newsitem.title: USA: Dollar recovers to end slightly higher in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dollar recovers to end slightly higher in U.S..

text.p: The dollar ended marginally higher versus the mark and yen, recovering from a spate of profit-taking after U.S. elections, experts said.

Speculation that voters would re-elect President Bill Clinton but keep Congress controlled by Republicans had boosted the dollar on Tuesday. Confirmation of this outcome initially prompted traders to dump dollars.

"It was a type of day to see some consolidation, some profit-taking, for the dollar to base and then to try and go higher," said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
The dollar stuck to narrow ranges on Wednesday. It dipped in New York to 1.5140 marks and 113.70 yen before erasing losses to end slightly firmer.
The U.S. currency closed at 1.5180/85 marks and 113.92/02 yen, up from 1.5176/81 marks and 113.77/87 yen at the open.
Initially, reports of a sharp increase in Japan's trade surplus and fresh doubts that a single European currency will debut in 1999 as planned had pressured the dollar.
The Ministry of Finance reported Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus ballooned 22.1 percent in the first 20 days of October from the same period a year earlier.

"If it (the Japan trade surplus) continues that way, U.S. officials may be concerned about it (and) start talking the dollar down," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
Concern about the timely debut of a single European currency arose from rumors and reports released on Wednesday.

Talk circulated in the foreign exchange market that German investment house Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was preparing to tell customers it expected the single currency might be delayed by two-years, experts said.
The dollar had lost ground to the mark as the German currency is viewed as a safe haven when ever doubts increase that the single currency will not be launched on time.
But the rumors proved untrue.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell senior currency analyst Marc Chandler said the firm told clients the risk that European Monetary Union may be postponed or scuttled altogether has increased marginally.
However, the firm also said it still believes the odds favor a small group of countries going ahead with monetary union on schedule, Chandler added.
Separately, the European Monetary Institute released a report stating that a majority of member states do not currently fulfill the necessary conditions for the adoption of a single currency.

This stood in contrast to a European Commission report, also released on Wednesday, that painted a rosy outlook for economic growth next year and saw a vast majority of 12 nations in the European Union meeting the tests for a single currency.
"There's concern that European Monetary Union won't go forward and the money will run back into Germany," Refco's Malpede said.
In other trade, the dollar closed at 1.2770/80 Swiss francs, up from 1.2755/65 at the open.
Sterling ended little changed, closing at $1.6412/22 compared with $1.6406/11 at the open.
The dollar also finished nearly flat versus the Canadian currency, closing at C$1.3314/19 versus C$1.3315/20. The Australian dollar ended at $0.7915/20, up from $0.7911/16.
